summary:
Put piece `a` before piece `b` exactly when the string `a + b` is larger than `b + a`. This rule is a consistent
ordering, so sorting the pieces (as strings) by it and joining gives the largest number. Answer `"0"` if the
result starts with 0 (all pieces were 0). O(n log n · L) for L digits.

question.md:
Arrange all the number pieces side by side to make the largest possible number, returned as a string with no
leading zeros.

- **Every piece is used**, each exactly once.
- **Plain numeric order fails:** 30 is bigger than 3, but `330` beats `303`.
- **All zeros** must give `"0"`, not `"000"`.

think.md:
Pieces `[30, 3, 34, 5, 9]`. The best is `9534330`.

Think about just two pieces side by side, `a` then `b`. Swapping them only changes that stretch of digits,
`a + b` versus `b + a`, which have the same length. So `a` belongs first exactly when `a + b > b + a`. This
pairwise rule turns out to be transitive (a proper ordering), so a sort with it arranges every pair correctly
at once.

approaches.title: Bubble sort with the glue rule

idea.md: Turn pieces into strings. Keep passing over the list, swapping neighbours whenever `b + a > a + b`, until a pass makes no swap.

build: Repeat passes with neighbour swaps until stable.

notes.c: Keep the numbers; the rule prints both glued orders to compare them.

lines.text: Pass over the pieces until nothing moves.
`b` should come first when `b + a` is the bigger number. Both glued strings have the same length, so comparing them as text compares them as numbers.
Join; if the biggest arrangement starts with 0, every piece was 0.

complexity.md: **Time O(n² · L)** comparisons of glued strings. **Space O(n · L).**

walk.title: Bubble sort with the rule 'a goes before b when a+b is the bigger number'. Repeatedly swap neighbours that break the rule.

limits.md: Bubble sort is quadratic: 10⁴ pieces means ~10⁸ string comparisons. The rule is a valid ordering, so any O(n log n) sort can use it.

idea.md: Sort the strings with the comparator `a before b ⟺ a + b > b + a`, join them, and return `"0"` if the result starts with 0.

code.python:
import functools

class Solution:
    def largestNumber(self, pieces: List[int]) -> str:
        s = [str(p) for p in pieces]
        rule = lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else (1 if a + b < b + a else 0)
        s.sort(key=functools.cmp_to_key(rule))
        out = "".join(s)
        return "0" if out[0] == "0" else out

notes.c: Keep the numbers; the comparator prints them glued both ways.

lines.text: `a` before `b` when `a + b` is the bigger number (same length, so text comparison works).

notes.java: Comparing `b + a` with `a + b` puts the larger glued order first.
notes.cpp: The comparator returns true when `a` should come first.
notes.c: `strcmp(y, x)` is negative when `x = a b` is bigger, which puts `a` first.

lines.text: Any comparison sort works, because the rule is a consistent ordering.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n · L)** with L ≤ 10 digits per piece. **Space O(n · L).**

steps.text: Why not just sort by digits? '3' vs '30': '330' beats '303', so 3 goes first, even though 30 is bigger.
Sort every piece with the rule: ['9', '5', '34', '3', '30'].

walk.title: Compare two pieces by gluing them both ways: put first whichever glued order makes the bigger number. Sort with that rule.

takeaways.md:
- When the best order depends on **how two items combine**, compare them by combining both ways.
- Exchange argument: if swapping two neighbours never helps, the arrangement is optimal.
- Watch the edge case where the "number" is all zeros.
